title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "‘The truth is that such a four-day week has many attractions but it will not be appropriate in every instance,’ says Professor Hazel."
Why: Professor Hazel's statement that a four-day week "will not be appropriate in every instance" directly matches the prompt's claim that a workplace initiative "may not be suitable for all businesses".

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "Anthropologists calculate that in the Stone Age, approximately one to two million years ago, the ancestors of modern humans worked on average two or three hours a day hunting and gathering food."
Why: The passage calculates that "the ancestors of modern humans" (ancient humans) worked "two or three hours a day", which provides an estimate of their working time.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Roland Gillespie, workplace relations minister in the New Zealand government, described the findings as ‘enormously encouraging’ and said that he was keen to see businesses experiment with similar new and improved work models."
Why: Roland Gillespie is a politician ("workplace relations minister") who expresses interest in changing how work is organized by encouraging businesses to try "new and improved work models".

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "Faisal Hadi, a lecturer in sociology, argues that the term work–life balance implies that the two represent distinct aspects of life that are easily separable."
Why: Faisal Hadi explains that the popular expression "work–life balance" oversimplifies a complex situation by falsely suggesting that work and life can be neatly separated.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "The chief executive of Certified Life, Tane Robinson, says that the four-day week boosted the firm’s reputation and made it easier to retain staff who might otherwise have moved on."
Why: Tane Robinson notes that the trial improved the public image of the business (boosted its reputation) and encouraged employees to remain with the company (retain staff).

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Says Deng, ‘Our research found that when employees have greater individual choice and responsibility for their work time, they still devote some of those “free” hours to fulfilling their normal working roles."
Why: Carla Deng provides research evidence showing that staff who are granted flexible personal time choose to spend some of those hours completing work that benefits the company.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "However, psychologist Dr Gina McDowell argues that the problem of stress caused by working too many hours still doesn’t receive sufficient recognition and ought to be addressed with greater commitment by executives, employees and academics."
Why: Dr Gina McDowell stresses that working excessive hours is a serious problem that lacks adequate recognition and requires greater commitment from everyone involved.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Lead researcher Dr Hannah Graham says that the experiment produced such positive results partly because employees were given a role in decision-making throughout it."
Why: Dr Hannah Graham identifies involving staff in decision-making at every stage of the experiment as a key factor behind its successful results.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "The experiment was conducted at Certified Life, a firm which has sold insurance for more than six decades."
Why: The passage notes that Certified Life "sold insurance", which directly answers what service was provided by the company involved in the experiment.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "The 240 employees at Certified Life completed surveys at the beginning and end of the experiment to provide information for the study."
Why: The question asks for the research method used to "gather data", which matches the passage phrase "provide information for the study" via "surveys".

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Furthermore, cooperation between employees was seen to improve significantly when working shorter hours and team cohesion was significantly enhanced, according to the supervisors."
Why: The phrase "staff worked together more closely" paraphrases "cooperation between employees was seen to improve... and team cohesion was significantly enhanced", which was reported "according to the supervisors".

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Quite apart from the benefits at Certified Life, Dr Graham also suggests that such schemes might address the issue of congestion in major cities by restricting the numbers going to work each day."
Why: The question asks about a problem outside the workplace (an issue in "major cities") that shorter hours could address, which Dr Graham identifies as "congestion".

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "He hits the ball with the tranquility of his perfected autopilot."
Why: Option C restates performing on "perfected autopilot" as acting "without conscious thought".

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "These networks of cells are the bodily ‘sentences’ we use every day, the ones our brain has chosen to retain and refine."
Why: Option B restates "networks of cells" as "a pattern of connected cells".

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Rather, we watch sport for the feeling, the human drama."
Why: Option A restates watching sport "for the feeling, the human drama" as watching to "experience strong positive emotions".

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "It turns out that watching a great golfer makes us better golfers, and watching a great sprinter actually makes us run faster."
Why: This sentence makes a clear claim that observing top athletes directly leads to an improvement in one's own performance.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "By letting spectators share in the motions of victory, they also allow us to share in their feelings."
Why: This explains that watching sports is emotionally satisfying because mirror neurons enable viewers to experience the feelings of the athletes.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Humans have an even more elaborate mirror neuron system."
Why: This sentence directly compares human mirror neurons to the animal (monkey) system described previously, noting that the human system is more elaborate.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "This phenomenon of neural mirroring was first discovered in 1954, when two French physiologists, Gastaut and Berf, found that the brains of humans vibrate with two distinct wavelengths, alpha and mu."
Why: This sentence details the initial discovery ("first discovered in 1954") of brain activity related to neural mirroring.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "This is because most novices swing with their consciousness, using an area of the brain next to the premotor cortex."
Why: This sentence explains why beginners ("novices") find athletic movements difficult, linking their struggle to relying on conscious brain areas.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "The best athletes are those with a premotor cortex capable of imagining the movements of victory, together with the physical properties to make those movements real."
Why: This sentence states that achieving sporting excellence requires combining neural mirroring ("imagining the movements") with physical traits ("physical properties").

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "This phenomenon of neural mirroring was first discovered in 1954, when two French physiologists, Gastaut and Berf, found that the brains of humans vibrate with two distinct wavelengths, alpha and mu."
Why: The passage identifies Gastaut and Berf as French physiologists, but the writer never mentions whether they were also sports players.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "If we are staring at a photograph, a fixed image of a runner mid-stride, our mirror neurons are totally silent."
Why: The question claims looking at a photograph can activate mirror neurons, but the writer states that mirror neurons are "totally silent" when looking at a photograph.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Humans have an even more elaborate mirror neuron system."
Why: The question states that monkeys have a more complex system than humans, but the writer explicitly claims humans have an "even more elaborate" mirror neuron system.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "This is because most novices swing with their consciousness, using an area of the brain next to the premotor cortex."
Why: The writer explains that novices (inexpert sports players) swing with their consciousness, meaning they are consciously aware of their physical movements rather than acting automatically.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "It is active when your bodies are still and disappears whenever you do something active, like playing a sport or changing the TV channel."
Why: The writer confirms that the mu system disappears (stops being active) whenever a person is engaged in an active task.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Ryan Schmidt, the director of human resources at MEdia, says that ‘productivity in the economy generally has increased significantly over the last 50 years but there’s a common perception in the workforce that standards of living have not kept pace."
Why: This sentence mentions that economic productivity has increased significantly (people working harder), but workers perceive that standards of living have not kept pace (their lives have not improved).

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "Only natural processes, such as volcanic eruptions and variations in solar output, caused periods of relative warming and cooling."
Why: The passage explains that before modern industrialisation, "Only natural processes" affected temperature variations and climate change.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "This disparity in warming between the poles and the tropics is a phenomenon known as polar amplification."
Why: The term "polar amplification" refers to the disparity or difference between warming at the poles and in the tropics.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Fresh snow is the brightest natural surface on Earth, as it reflects nearly 85% of solar radiation that hits it."
Why: The verb "reflects" describes what fresh snow does to 85% (most) of the solar radiation (sunlight) that hits it.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "In the springtime, this ice melts and exposes the dark ocean underneath, which leads to warming of the region, and this warming melts even more ice, resulting in a positive feedback loop."
Why: The text explicitly states that sea ice melts "In the springtime", which initiates regional warming.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "The level of melting of the Greenland ice sheet is a major indicator of potential sea level rise; if it completely melts, global sea levels could rise by as much as 6 metres, endangering coastal cities and small island nations while making dangerous weather events, such as floods and hurricanes, even more deadly."
Why: The passage lists "coastal cities" along with small island nations as places endangered if the Greenland ice sheet melts.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "The most troubling effect of this feedback loop is the release of methane into the atmosphere."
Why: The passage identifies the release (leakage) of "methane" into the atmosphere as the most troubling effect or worry.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In fact, the average temperature of Antarctica has not changed in the last several decades, despite an increase in the concentration of greenhouse gases."
Why: The passage states that the average temperature of Antarctica "has not changed", which contradicts the claim in the statement that rising greenhouse gases "have increased temperatures".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "In autumn, large storms in the open ocean create more waves that cause the Arctic waters to mix with warmer waters, which increases the heat absorbed in the summer, making ice formation more difficult again in the autumn."
Why: The passage explains that wave action in autumn makes ice formation harder, but it does not state whether wave action accelerates sea ice melting during the summer.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "The level of melting of the Greenland ice sheet is a major indicator of potential sea level rise; if it completely melts, global sea levels could rise by as much as 6 metres, endangering coastal cities and small island nations while making dangerous weather events, such as floods and hurricanes, even more deadly."
Why: The passage confirms that if the Greenland ice sheet melts completely, a 6-metre sea level rise would occur, "endangering coastal cities and small island nations".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "The Arctic land that was once covered in snow during the summer has shrunk in size significantly, and this darker land absorbs more heat than before, further warming the Arctic and the rest of the planet."
Why: The passage states that the darker exposed land absorbs "more heat than before", directly contradicting the statement's claim that it absorbs "less heat".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "However, if the soil is waterlogged, fermentation occurs and this discharges a gas called methane."
Why: The passage shows that dry soil releases mostly carbon dioxide, but when the soil is "waterlogged" (contains high amounts of water), methane is released instead.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "As the situation nears its tipping point, a global campaign is underway to actually remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere manually, using techniques such as Direct Air Capture, a process of capturing carbon dioxide directly from the air surrounding us, as opposed to direct capture from point sources, such as factories, and sequestering this carbon directly or utilizing it for other purposes."
Why: The passage mentions that Direct Air Capture is being used to remove carbon dioxide, but it does not say that it is the "most effective" method.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "This is what plants do naturally, but Direct Air Capture does it much more rapidly and requires less land space."
Why: The passage states that Direct Air Capture captures carbon dioxide "much more rapidly and requires less land space" than plants, showing it is more efficient.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Dolls constructed of flat pieces of wood, painted with various designs, and with ‘hair’ made of clay, have often been found in Egyptian graves dating back to 2000 BC."
Why: The text explicitly states that these Egyptian dolls had "'hair' made of clay", which directly completes the note.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Girls from ancient Greece and Rome offered their wooden dolls to goddesses after they were too ‘grown-up’ to play with dolls."
Why: The passage explains that older girls offered (gave) their dolls to "goddesses".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "That ideal led to the creation of dolls with movable limbs and removable garments, dating back to 600 BC."
Why: The phrase "movable limbs" in the text matches the note's description of parts "that could be put in different positions".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "In addition to wooden dolls, wax dolls grew in popularity in the 17th and 18th centuries."
Why: The text states that "wax dolls" became popular during the 17th and 18th centuries, filling the gap for the material used.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Wax modellers would model a doll’s head in wax or clay, and then cover it with plaster to create a mould."
Why: The passage states that modellers covered the doll's head with "plaster" to make the mould.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 12
Quote: "Composition is a collective term for mixtures of pulped wood or paper that were used to make doll heads and bodies."
Why: The text introduces "Composition" as the collective term (or new group) for these pulped mixtures developed in the 1800s.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Bisque, which is porcelain fired twice with colour added to it after the first firing, looked more like skin than china did."
Why: The passage states that bisque looked more like skin than china did, making it more realistic. This contradicts the statement that bisque dolls appeared less realistic than china dolls.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "Although the French dolls were unrivalled in their artistry, German bisque dolls became quite popular because they were not as expensive."
Why: The text states that German bisque dolls were not as expensive as French dolls, which means French dolls tended to cost more.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "For many centuries, rag dolls were made by mothers for their children."
Why: The passage says rag dolls existed for many centuries before 1850, when commercial production began. This contradicts the claim that the first rag dolls were made in the 1850s.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "Cloth doll refers to a subset of rag dolls made of linen or cotton."
Why: The text specifies that cloth dolls are defined as rag dolls made specifically of linen or cotton.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 11
Quote: "However, celluloid fell out of favour because of its extreme flammability and propensity to fade in bright light."
Why: The passage notes that celluloid had a propensity to fade in bright light, which means it tended to lose its colour.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 12
Quote: "They resembled composition dolls, but they were much more durable."
Why: The text states that hard plastic dolls from the 1940s were much more durable than composition dolls. This contradicts the claim that composition dolls lasted longer.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Dolls through the ages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 12
Quote: "Although most dolls are now mass-manufactured using these modern materials, many modern doll makers are still using the traditional materials of the past to make collectible dolls."
Why: While collectible dolls are mentioned, the passage does not mention whether collectors prefer dolls dressed in their original clothing.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Herding
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "However, recurring drought throughout Western Asia in the 1960s limited fertile areas, and oil production in Egypt and Saudi Arabia further reduced land available for grazing."
Why: The note lists two causes for the Bedouin becoming semi-nomadic: "___ and oil production". The passage states that "recurring drought" and "oil production" led to this change, making "drought" the correct word.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Herding
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "However, young people have recently been rejecting this way of life and are instead moving to cities in search of an easier life."
Why: The note states that young members "prefer to live in the ___", which corresponds to "moving to cities" in the passage.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Herding
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "For centuries, the Sami have herded reindeer as a principal means of livelihood, supplemented by fishing and trapping."
Why: The note lists three methods of survival: "herding, ___ and catching wild animals". The passage mentions herding, "fishing", and "trapping" (catching wild animals), so "fishing" completes the list.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Herding
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Trees are also being cut down for the timber industry, and mines are being dug to extract minerals, all of which have a serious impact on grazing land."
Why: The note refers to land being exploited for "wood and ___". The text matches "wood" to "timber" (from cut-down trees) and mentions extracting "minerals" from mines.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Herding
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Another type of herding in mountainous regions is called transhumance."
Why: The note describes transhumance as taking place in "areas which are ___", matching the text's description of "mountainous regions".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Herding
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Unlike nomads, these herders move their animals between the same areas and live in fixed settlements."
Why: The phrase "permanent ___" in the note directly paraphrases "fixed settlements" from the text.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Herding
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "Shepherds lead herds to the middle pastures during the spring."
Why: The note asks when animals spend time in the middle pastures. The text specifies that shepherds lead herds there "during the spring".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The plants that produce rubber are spread right across the globe, and grow in many different habitats."
Why: The statement claims rubber plants grow "only in certain regions", which contradicts the passage stating they are "spread right across the globe".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The Indians of South America appear to be the first people to have understood the properties of rubber, and the Aztecs of what is now Mexico were the first to be recorded using the substance; a wall painting dating back to the sixth century depicts a scene of a tributary offering of crude rubber."
Why: The passage confirms that crude rubber was recorded being used in what is now Mexico as early as the sixth century.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Rubber was also used to make raincoats, shoes, jars, torches and musical instruments, all of which must have been made from the indigenous Castilla elastica, as the Para plant now favoured for rubber cultivation does not grow in the Mexican region."
Why: The passage mentions both plants, but it does not compare the quality of rubber produced by Castilla elastica with that of the Para plant.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "However, no real interest in rubber was shown by any European until Charles de la Condamine, a French mathematician, published an account of his journey to South America in 1735."
Why: The passage explicitly states that European interest in rubber began when Charles de la Condamine, a French mathematician, published his journey account.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Then in 1839 the American Charles Goodyear discovered that it was possible to stabilise rubber by mixing it with sulphur while exposing it to heat – a process he called vulcanisation – and the full versatility of this extraordinary substance became apparent."
Why: The text states that Goodyear discovered vulcanisation, but it does not mention whether the discovery occurred by accident.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "The import levels of rubber over the nineteenth century bear witness to its irrepressible rise."
Why: The statement says imports fell during the nineteenth century, contradicting the passage which states they experienced an "irrepressible rise".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In 1818 a British medical student named James Syme first used rubber to make waterproof cloth."
Why: The question asks what was produced using rubber in 1818, and the passage states that James Syme "first used rubber to make waterproof cloth" in that year.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In 1820 Thomas Hancock, an English manufacturer of rubber goods such as driving belts, industrial rollers and rubber hoses, invented a machine he called the "pickle", which chewed up waste strips for re-use."
Why: The question refers to a machine invented in 1820 for recycling rubber. The passage describes Hancock's machine, which "chewed up waste strips for re-use", meaning recycling.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "They also became pliant when warm and rigid when cold."
Why: The question describes rubber products becoming "soft" (pliant) when warm and asks for the opposite state when cold. The passage states they became "rigid when cold".

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Then in 1839 the American Charles Goodyear discovered that it was possible to stabilise rubber by mixing it with sulphur while exposing it to heat – a process he called vulcanisation – and the full versatility of this extraordinary substance became apparent."
Why: The question asks what new process in 1839 increased rubber's potential. The passage states that Goodyear discovered it was possible to "stabilise rubber" in 1839.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "It played an important role in the Industrial Revolution, being employed in the steam engines found in factories, mills, mines and railways."
Why: The question asks what rubber was used in during the Industrial Revolution. The passage states it was "employed in the steam engines" during this period.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "One of the most important rubber inventions was made in 1888, when an Irishman called John Boyd Dunlop produced the first pneumatic tyre."
Why: The question asks what was developed in 1888. The passage states that Dunlop "produced the first pneumatic tyre" in that year.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Rubber
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "In 1895 Dunlop’s tyres were first used in motor cars, and with the mass production of cars just over the horizon the rubber industry had never looked healthier."
Why: The question asks what began a few years after 1888 (referring to the motor car). The passage mentions "the mass production of cars" as being "just over the horizon" around 1895, indicating its beginning.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Scented Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Floral scent has a strong impact on the economic success of many agricultural crops that rely on insect pollinators, including fruit trees such as the bee-pollinated cherry, apple, apricot, and peach, as well as vegetables and tropical plants such as the papaya."
Why: This sentence lists specific food plants like cherry, apple, and papaya, and states they "rely on insect pollinators," which means they need insects to be productive.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Scented Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Clearly, a more refined strategy is needed; genetic manipulation of scents, for example, would allow growers to regulate the types of insect pollinators and the frequency of their visits."
Why: This sentence explains that "genetic manipulation of scents" (a genetic experiment) would help "regulate the types of insect pollinators and the frequency of their visits," thereby assisting plant reproduction.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Scented Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "The next generation of experiments, already in progress, will include more sophisticated schemes that target the expression of scent specifically to flowers or other organs, such as special glands that can store antibacterial or herbivore-repellent compounds."
Why: This sentence describes "experiments, already in progress" (current research) aimed at restoring scent to flowers, which would benefit the "flower industry" mentioned earlier in the paragraph.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Scented Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Insects are the most common animals to interact with plants in this way, and most insects detect volatile compounds through the extremely sensitive antennae on their heads."
Why: This sentence explains that insects "detect volatile compounds through the extremely sensitive antennae on their heads," describing the mechanism by which they perceive these compounds.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Scented Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Humans have recognized and taken advantage of these plant-derived antibacterials since antiquity, when they were used to slow the spoilage of food."
Why: The phrase "slow the spoilage of food" means to prevent food from decaying, which is directly restated by option D.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Scented Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "In the rainforest tree Leonardoxa africana, for example, ants of the species Petalomyrmex phylax are attracted to young leaves because they emit high levels of the volatile compound methyl salicylate, a substance that ants need to use as an antiseptic in their nests; coincidentally, the ants attack any herbivorous insects that they encounter."
Why: The passage states that the tree attracts ants, and these ants then "attack any herbivorous insects," meaning they are an enemy of the plant-eating insects, as described in option A.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Scented Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "In the rainforest tree Leonardoxa africana, for example, ants of the species Petalomyrmex phylax are attracted to young leaves because they emit high levels of the volatile compound methyl salicylate, a substance that ants need to use as an antiseptic in their nests; coincidentally, the ants attack any herbivorous insects that they encounter."
Why: The passage states that methyl salicylate attracts ants (A), helps the tree deter herbivores (B), and is used by ants as an antiseptic (C). It does not mention that it helps herbivorous insects find food; in fact, it helps deter them, making option D the statement that is NOT true.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Scented Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "This problem has been made worse in the United States by recent epidemics that have infected and killed many honeybees, the major insect pollinator."
Why: The passage explicitly states that epidemics have "infected and killed many honeybees," which means their numbers have been reduced by disease, as stated in option B.

title: Reading Passage 1 - Scented Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Some preliminary experiments have already been carried out, but for technical reasons the scent was present in every part of the plant, rather than being localized in the flower, and the level of intensity of fragrance was below the threshold of detection for the human nose."
Why: The passage states that "the level of intensity of fragrance was below the threshold of detection for the human nose," meaning the scent was not strong enough for people to smell, which is restated by option C.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "In 1882, domestic electricity at last became a possibility when Thomas Edison's company started providing electricity on a commercial basis."
Why: The question asks for the year electricity was supplied to homeowners for the first time. The quote states that in 1882, domestic electricity became a possibility when Edison's company started providing it commercially.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "The electric iron appeared in 1893, the electric vacuum cleaner in 1901, the electric washing machine in 1909, and the electric dishwasher in 1918."
Why: The question asks for the last electrical appliance to appear in the 1889-1918 period. The quote lists the electric dishwasher in 1918 as the final item in this sequence.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4

title: Reading Passage 1 - The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "In that year, people spent $175 million on them."
Why: The question asks for the year when consumer spending on electrical appliances totalled $175m. The sentence immediately preceding the quote states "By 1917...", making "that year" refer to 1917.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Much the same happened with a small company called Frigidaire, founded in 1918, which saw an opening for a refrigerator designed for the home and so successfully seized the opportunity that the name almost became generic, although it took until 1927 for General Electric to produce the first million-selling model."
Why: The question asks for the domestic appliance that General Electric produced a million-selling model of in 1927. The quote states that in 1927, General Electric produced the first million-selling model of a "refrigerator".

title: Reading Passage 1 - The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "The proportion would have been higher still except that rural electrification took so long to complete; even by 1946, as little as half of US farms had electricity."
Why: The question asks what specific group had only 50% electrification by 1946. The quote states that "even by 1946, as little as half of US farms had electricity."

title: Reading Passage 1 - The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "By 1926, there was a radio in five per cent of homes, and by the end of that decade, with almost every household owning at least one, market saturation was practically complete."
Why: The question asks what product was in nearly every home by 1930 (the end of the decade). The quote states that "by the end of that decade" (the 1920s), "almost every household owning at least one" radio.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "The concept of the national park originated in America, though it was quickly replicated by similar parks in Canada, Finland, New Zealand, Australia, and elsewhere."
Why: The passage states that the concept of national parks originated in America, and was then copied by other countries, which is the opposite of the statement.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "Yellowstone comprises some 3,500 square miles of wilderness and today attracts more than four million visitors a year."
Why: The passage states how many visitors Yellowstone attracts but does not compare this number to other national parks to say if it is the most frequently visited.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "They are administered by the National Parks Service (NPS), which also manages significant monuments and historic structures such as the Statue of Liberty, the Gettysburg Museum, and Ford’s Theatre, where President Lincoln was assassinated."
Why: The passage states that the NPS manages "significant monuments and historic structures" in addition to the national parks, confirming its responsibility for both buildings and natural landscapes.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "In 1832, the painter George Catlin dreamed of creating ‘a nation’s park’ to preserve the grasslands in the state of South Dakota."
Why: The passage mentions Catlin's proposal but does not provide any information about whether he was criticised for it.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Four years later, the writer Ralph Waldo Emerson published an important essay entitled Nature, in which he argued that natural landscapes should be protected rather than exploited for agriculture and commerce."
Why: The passage states that Emerson argued natural landscapes should be "protected rather than exploited for agriculture and commerce," which means he did not believe farms and businesses should use land freely.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The creation of a public park in the Yosemite Valley was directly the result of his work."
Why: The passage directly states that the creation of a public park in the Yosemite Valley was "directly the result of his work," confirming Olmsted's role in its establishment.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "The Yellowstone National Park not only preserved the headwaters of the Mississippi, Colorado, and Snake rivers, but also provided a sanctuary for countless endangered species by imposing a ban on hunting in all its forms."
Why: The phrase "imposing a ban on hunting in all its forms" directly tells us that "every type of hunting was prohibited" in Yellowstone Park.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In recognition of the difficulties of running these vast wilderness areas, their management was for many years placed in the hands of the military, rather than the federal or state government."
Why: The question states that parks were "administered by" a group, and the passage uses "management" as a synonym for administration, stating it was "placed in the hands of the military".

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Increasingly, these ran through even the most remote areas, where many parks were located, making tourism possible in these locations for the very first time."
Why: The passage explains that railroads "making tourism possible" directly relates to the idea that the railroad system "encouraged new kinds of tourism".

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Nathaniel Langford was instrumental in setting up Yellowstone and saw the park as an ideal opportunity for the education of ordinary citizens in all aspects of the natural world and environmental conservation, which was his number one priority."
Why: Langford's "number one priority" was "the education of ordinary citizens", which matches the question's "public education" as the "most important role".

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "However, arguably even more important was Mather’s transformation of the hitherto poorly managed finances of the parks."
Why: The passage states that Mather's "transformation of the hitherto poorly managed finances" means he "greatly improved the finances" of the parks.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "However, the controversial decision to permit the construction of dams in national parks was made on the basis that the resulting supplies of water and hydroelectric power would be in the public interest."
Why: The phrase "permit the construction of dams" directly means that the NPS "allowed some dams to be built" in national parks.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Then in the 1930s, the number of visitors expanded dramatically, largely because mass-produced automobiles became affordable, allowing ever more city-dwellers to reach the park network."
Why: The passage explains that in the 1930s, the "number of visitors expanded dramatically" (popularity increased) because "automobiles became affordable" (availability of automobiles).

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "Though Rome draws tourists from around the world to its many impressive sites, one notable monument there has never attracted nearly as much interest: The Pyramid of Cestius."
Why: The passage states that the Pyramid of Cestius has *never* attracted nearly as much interest as other sites, which contradicts the idea that it has *always* been popular.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The only one left standing, the Pyramid of Cestius, was designed as the burial pyramid for a Roman politician named Caius Cestius, who ordered that the building work be completed within a period of 330 days."
Why: The passage states Cestius ordered the work to be completed within 330 days and gives the construction dates, but it does not provide any information about when Cestius died in relation to the completion of the pyramid.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "By the Middle Ages, the pyramid was covered in vegetation and thick dirt, and popular myth had developed that it might be a tomb for one of the twin brothers Romulus and Remus, who were regarded as the men who had established the city of Rome."
Why: The passage states that in the Middle Ages, a popular myth was that the pyramid might be a tomb for Romulus and Remus, who were regarded as the men who had established the city of Rome.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Today, the foundations of Cestius pyramid rest below street level near an intersection with heavy traffic, so that passing tourists and residents could easily fail to notice its full height of 119 feet."
Why: The passage states that passing tourists and residents could *easily fail to notice* the pyramid's full height, which contradicts the idea that they would immediately notice it.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Work began at the site shortly after Yagi signed an official agreement with the Special Superintendency for the Archaeological Heritage of Rome, and was completed ahead of schedule thanks to his 2-million-euro contribution."
Why: The passage states that the work on the pyramid "was completed ahead of schedule," which means it finished earlier than expected.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "We know from the writings of earlier visitors that there used to be more here, but the majority have disappeared over time."
Why: The passage states that while some frescoes remain, "the majority have disappeared over time," which contradicts the idea that most of them have survived.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Cestius pyramid had a layer of white Carrara marble on the outside, and was constructed from brick held together by a basic kind of cement on the inside."
Why: The passage lists the materials used for construction, and 'brick' is one of them, fitting the gap alongside marble and cement.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "One of the things that strikes you when you look at the pyramid is how steep it is, so that the shape of Cestius' pyramid is quite unlike that of typical Egyptian ones."
Why: The sentence directly states that the 'shape' of Cestius' pyramid is different from Egyptian ones, matching the description in the question.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "At the time of its construction, since there was a strict Roman law prohibiting the placement of tombs within the city itself, the Pyramid of Cestius would have stood in countryside."
Why: The passage explains that due to a law against tombs in the city, the pyramid was originally built in the 'countryside'.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "During excavations, when trees and plants were cleared away, two marble bases were found in front of the pyramid, as well as fragments of bronze statues that had once stood on them on either side of the pyramid."
Why: The question mentions 'broken' items found, and the passage refers to 'fragments of bronze statues' discovered during the 1660s restoration.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "The people employed to excavate the pyramid did not find the urn that would have contained Cestius' remains, but they did come across a tunnel."
Why: The passage states that a 'tunnel' was found, which suggested that robbers might have removed the tomb's contents.

title: Reading Passage 1 - The Pyramid of Cestius
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "The white exterior of the Pyramid of Cestius will have to be cleaned every few months to remove the layer of urban pollution."
Why: The passage explains that climbers will be employed to clean the pyramid to remove 'urban pollution', which directly answers what they are getting rid of.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration

Why: This sentence explains that Farmers was purchased by the James Pascoe Group, which is described as "owned by David and Annie Norman," indicating it is a privately owned (family) company.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1

Why: The question asks what Farmers was first founded as, and the passage states Robert Laidlaw established a 'mail-order company' in Auckland.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "Branch expansion: purchase of Green and Colebrook chain store; further provincial stores in Auckland and Waikato to follow."
Why: The question mentions Farmers buying "one ___ then another", and the passage describes the "purchase of Green and Colebrook chain store" as part of its expansion.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1

Why: The question asks for a city where Farmers set up during overseas expansion, listing New York, and the passage mentions 'London and New York buying offices'.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Farmers was once the home of genteel tearooms, children's playgrounds, and an annual sale to celebrate the birthday of Hector the Parrot (the store mascot died, aged 131, in the 1970s; his stuffed remains still occupy pride of place at the company's head office)."
Why: The question asks what Farmers held annually for the parrot, and the passage states "an annual sale to celebrate the birthday of Hector the Parrot".

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "I think, once, Farmers was like a big family and all of the people who worked for it felt they were building something which would ultimately be to their benefit and to the benefit of New Zealand..."
Why: The question asks what Lincoln Laidlaw thought Farmers was like for employees, and he states, "Farmers was like a big family" and beneficial for New Zealand.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:

Why: Ian Hunter explicitly states that Farmers' money-back guarantee was the first of its kind in New Zealand, making it an unprecedented statement for a company in the country.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Farmers Centenary Celebration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "I think, once, Farmers was like a big family and all of the people who worked for it felt they were building something which would ultimately be to their benefit and to the benefit of New Zealand... then the business was being divided up and so that kind of family situation was dispelled and it hasn't been recovered."
Why: Lincoln Laidlaw describes how the company's original "family situation" was "dispelled" after it was divided up, indicating a significant change in the company's character.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Jan Elsner, a psychologist who specialises in executive coaching, says that doing well on a demanding workload is typical of senior executives."
Why: Jan Elsner states that senior executives often "do well" with demanding workloads, indicating a positive reaction to stress.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "I'll promise a client that I'll do something tomorrow, and then I'll promise another client that I'll do the same thing, when I know it's not going to happen."
Why: Neil Plumridge describes how over-promising to clients, in an attempt to please them, leads to stress when he cannot deliver.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "He also relies on the advice of colleagues, saying that his peers coach each other on business problems: "Just a fresh pair of eyes over an issue can help," he states."
Why: Neil Plumridge explains that getting advice and coaching from colleagues helps him deal with business problems, implying it can relieve stress.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "His recent research shows that the major predictor of stress is the level of job control a person has."
Why: Tony LaMontagne's research identifies a lack of job control (independence) as the primary cause of stress.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "A study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology shows that people always believe that they will be less busy in the future."
Why: Gal Zauberman and John Lynch's research indicates that people commonly have the misapprehension that their future workloads will be lighter.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "He knows he is doing too much when he gets less than six hours' sleep for three consecutive nights, when he is constantly having to reschedule appointments, and when he misses a family birthday or anniversary."
Why: The passage lists insufficient sleep, rescheduling appointments, and missing family events as signs of an overloaded workload for Neil Plumridge. A lack of concentration on a task is not mentioned.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Neil Plumridge says he makes it a priority to work out what has to change: that might mean allocating extra staff to a job, allowing more time, or changing expectations."
Why: Neil Plumridge suggests allocating extra staff, allowing more time (extending deadlines), and changing expectations (rethinking what can be achieved). Taking more time off for sport or recreation is not suggested by him; in fact, the passage states experts advise against focusing on such 'relief'.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "She points to research showing that meditation can alter the biochemistry of the brain and the way that brains and bodies react to stress."
Why: Jan Elsner explains that meditation can "alter the biochemistry of the brain and the way that brains and bodies react to stress," which directly refers to changing the physical response to stress.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Figures for National Workers' Compensation (insurance against injury caused by work) show that stress causes the most lost time of any workplace injury: employees suffering stress are absent from work for an average of 16.6 weeks."
Why: The summary states that people take more time off due to stress than for any other ___. The passage explicitly says stress causes "the most lost time of any workplace injury," directly filling the gap.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Figures for National Workers' Compensation (insurance against injury caused by work) show that stress causes the most lost time of any workplace injury: employees suffering stress are absent from work for an average of 16.6 weeks."
Why: The question asks for the average time workers stay away due to stress. The passage states that "employees suffering stress are absent from work for an average of 16.6 weeks."

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "The Australian Government insurer reports that in 2003-2004, claims for stress-related psychological injury accounted for 7% of insurance claims, but almost 27% of the amount paid out in claim payments."
Why: The summary asks for the percentage of total insurance claims due to stress. The passage states that "claims for stress-related psychological injury accounted for 7% of insurance claims."

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Experts say the key to dealing with stress is not to focus on relief—a game of golf or a massage—but to reassess workloads."
Why: The summary mentions "physical therapies such as sport or ___". The passage lists "a game of golf or a massage" as examples of relief, and "sport" is a synonym for "a game of golf," making "massage" the missing item.

title: Reading Passage 2 - STRESS LESS
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Experts say the key to dealing with stress is not to focus on relief—a game of golf or a massage—but to reassess workloads."
Why: The summary suggests that physical therapies are less effective than "simply reviewing your ___". The passage states that the key to dealing with stress is "to reassess workloads," which matches the meaning of "reviewing your workloads."

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "Associate Professor Dieter Hochuli, a biologist at the University of Sydney, believes that ‘we need to understand how cities are changing the ecology of the systems they are built on, and how plants and animals are adapting to them’."
Why: This sentence explains the reason why natural scientists (ecologists and biologists) are interested in studying how plants and animals adapt to urban environments.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "The bird’s reputation for digging through inner-city bins and scavenging street garbage has not endeared it to the public."
Why: This sentence describes the white ibis as a creature that actively seeks out and consumes rubbish, earning it the nickname 'garbage turkey'.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "‘They’re a real winner in cities,’ Australian Museum ornithologist Richard Major says."
Why: This quote refers to the noisy miner bird, which, along with other omnivorous birds, has successfully adapted to and thrives in the urban environment, unlike some smaller native birds.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "Many invertebrates, such as the golden orb weaver spider and the blue triangle butterfly, also relish living in the city."
Why: This sentence introduces the main topic of the paragraph, which is how various invertebrates (including insects like butterflies and spiders) are thriving in the city.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "However, the rabbit-sized, long-nosed bandicoot has discovered the advantages of venturing out of Sydney Harbour National Park and into suburban gardens."
Why: This sentence describes the bandicoot, a small animal, changing its behaviour by moving from its natural park habitat into urban gardens, thereby expanding its territory.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Over 20 years, Leishman and her colleagues have shown how Sydney’s huge stretches of impermeable concrete, together with the stormwater system, have helped weeds infiltrate the few remaining pockets of bushland."
Why: This sentence explains how the urban environment (concrete, stormwater) encourages the spread of imported plant life (weeds), and the paragraph also mentions other non-native animals.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "‘We don’t know if it’s an overflow from the park, or if they’ve got particular survival traits that allow them to evade dogs and cats, and use the urban habitat that benefits them,’ she says."
Why: Catherine Price explicitly states that "we don't know" the reason for the bandicoot's movement into urban environments, indicating that the reason is not clear.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "‘We’re trying to determine whether it’s more food or the urban heat, as it’s up to four degrees warmer in the city.’"
Why: Dieter Hochuli's team is investigating if "urban heat" (hot weather) is a reason why golden orb spiders are "fatter and fitter," suggesting a positive effect on their health.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "‘The predominant driver in the decline of small birds is that we’ve made a suitable environment for native noisy miners.’"
Why: Richard Major explains that the environment created by residential gardens is "suitable" for noisy miners, but causes the "decline of small birds," showing that these gardens suit some species better than others.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "Associate Professor Dieter Hochuli, a biologist at the University of Sydney, believes that ‘we need to understand how cities are changing the ecology of the systems they are built on, and how plants and animals are adapting to them’."
Why: Dieter Hochuli's statement that "we need to understand" these changes emphasizes the vital importance of research into how the natural world responds to urban settings.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Non-native species such as black rodents, cockroaches and foxes have developed survival strategies too."
Why: The summary asks for an example of a non-native insect. The passage lists "cockroaches" as a non-native species that has developed survival strategies, fitting the description.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Over 20 years, Leishman and her colleagues have shown how Sydney’s huge stretches of impermeable concrete, together with the stormwater system, have helped weeds infiltrate the few remaining pockets of bushland."
Why: The summary states that Michelle Leishman has proven that "___ and its drainage network favour the growth of weeds". The passage directly links "Sydney’s huge stretches of impermeable concrete" and the "stormwater system" (drainage network) to helping weeds.

title: Reading Passage 2 - Surviving city life
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "As rain washes over backyards and roadways, it collects chemicals which enter the stormwater system, where it is piped to the edges of bushland."
Why: The summary mentions that "Sydney’s large areas of ___ gather as water passes from gardens and streets into the city drainage network". The passage explains that rain "collects chemicals" as it washes over "backyards and roadways" (gardens and streets) and enters the "stormwater system" (city drainage network).

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "The law influences all of us virtually all the time."
Why: This opening sentence introduces the core idea that the law touches nearly every aspect of our existence from birth to death, perfectly matching the heading about the law applying throughout our lives.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Today, by contrast, a vast number of people can read, and it is becoming easier for people to take an interest in law, and for the general population to help actually shape the law in many countries."
Why: The paragraph explains how higher literacy rates have enabled everyday people to engage with and actively help shape legislation, which corresponds directly to the public's increasing ability to influence the law.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "In our rapidly developing world, all sorts of skills and knowledge are valuable."
Why: The paragraph compares the essential nature of IT specialists and legal professionals in modern society, discussing different specialized fields of expertise required across various sectors.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "The number of laws has never been greater."
Why: This topic sentence is supported by statistics showing a massive increase in Acts of Parliament and statutory instruments, which directly illustrates the growth in laws over time.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "However, despite their important role in developing the rules, lawyers are not universally admired."
Why: The paragraph outlines the long-standing negative public perception and jokes directed at lawyers, which aligns with the heading about a negative regard for lawyers.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "But, in general, it is no more just to say that lawyers are bad because they make a living from people’s problems than it is to make the same accusation in respect of nurses or IT consultants."
Why: The paragraph defends the legal profession by explaining that many lawyers perform vital public law work, engage in routine drafting rather than conflict, and suffer from misunderstandings, thus giving reasons why it is unfair to criticise lawyers.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "But legal understanding is just as vital and as universally needed."
Why: This matches the statement that knowledge of the law is just as important as having computer skills, which is discussed in the comparison with IT professionals earlier in the paragraph.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "In other words, the lawyer is the only person who has read and made sense of the rules."
Why: This explains why society cannot function effectively without legal experts, as lawyers are uniquely equipped to understand the rules that govern our everyday activities.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "People sometimes make comments that characterise lawyers as professionals whose concerns put personal reward above truth, or who gain financially from misfortune."
Why: The summary states that lawyers are accused of ignoring something in favor of making money; the passage matches this by stating their concerns put "personal reward above truth".

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "There are undoubtedly lawyers that would fit that bill, just as there are some scientists, journalists and others in that category."
Why: The text compares lawyers who prioritize money to people in other professions, specifically naming scientists and "journalists" to fill the gap.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "But, in general, it is no more just to say that lawyers are bad because they make a living from people’s problems than it is to make the same accusation in respect of nurses or IT consultants."
Why: The sentence defends lawyers by comparing them to "nurses" or IT consultants (referred to as IT staff in the summary) who also make a living from people's problems.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Moreover, much legal work has nothing to do with conflict or misfortune, but is primarily concerned with drafting documents."
Why: The summary contrasts dealing with misfortunes by noting that lawyers spend a lot of time writing "documents".

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Others, including Ekman, argue that the face can display information about emotions, but they admit that it is not reliable one hundred percent of the time."
Why: This sentence explains that facial expressions are "not reliable one hundred percent of the time," which matches the idea that they do not always provide a true guide to feelings.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "So a smile may prompt people to approach, a scowl may warn them to stay away, and a look of sadness may elicit words of sympathy and reassurance."
Why: The text gives specific examples of how different facial expressions—a smile, a scowl, and a look of sadness—cause other people to take specific actions in response.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "At times, though, it may be uncomfortable or inconvenient for us to let others know our emotions."
Why: This sentence outlines the reasons (feeling "uncomfortable or inconvenient") why people might choose to hide their true emotions.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "His studies find that expressions occur most often during pivotal points — the turning points in social interactions — during greetings, social crises, or times of appeasement, for example."
Why: The text lists specific situations ("greetings, social crises, or times of appeasement") as examples of times when facial expressions happen most frequently.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "He found, for example, that a smile represented joy and a scowl represented anger. In fact, since the 1970s Ekman has dominated the field of emotion research with his theory that when an emotion occurs, a large number of electrical impulses also occur, creating specific facial expressions and other physiological changes, such as increased or decreased heart rate or heightened blood pressure."
Why: This sentence details internal bodily changes that happen with emotion, specifically citing "increased or decreased heart rate or heightened blood pressure."

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "The face is a component [of emotion], but to make it the centre of study of the human being experiencing an emotion is like saying the only thing you need to study in a car is the transmission."
Why: Joseph Campos uses the analogy of studying just the transmission of a car to describe how looking only at the face in emotion research is like studying just one part of a larger system.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Expressions evolved to set off certain behaviours in other people, says Fridlund."
Why: Alan Fridlund argues that facial expressions developed ("evolved") to trigger specific reactions or behaviours in others.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "The area of dispute between Fridlund and Ekman draws attention away from their major areas of agreement, says Joseph Campos of the University of California."
Why: Joseph Campos points out that despite their disagreements on certain matters, Ekman and Fridlund fundamentally share major areas of agreement.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "She believes there are many situations where emotion is experienced, yet no basic facial expression is displayed."
Why: Linda Camras notes that emotions can occur without a matching facial expression, and vice versa, showing they can exist independently.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "Although much work on the emotions relies on a link between facial expression and emotions, psychologist James Russell of the University of British Columbia says there is very little evidence supporting such a connection."
Why: James Russell states that there is very little evidence to prove a direct connection between facial expressions and true emotions.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "So a smile may prompt people to approach, a scowl may warn them to stay away, and a look of sadness may elicit words of sympathy and reassurance."
Why: The question asks what facial expression might invite people to come nearer ("approach"), and the passage states that a "smile" prompts people to approach.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Even when people are alone they are holding a dialogue with another person internally, or imagining themselves in a social situation."
Why: The question notes that we use facial expressions when we are by ourselves because we are communicating with someone in our minds, which matches the passage's description of holding a "dialogue" internally.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "Thus Fridlund thinks of facial expressions as tools for influencing social interactions, a view which, he claims, enables us to begin predicting when certain facial expressions will occur."
Why: The question describes facial expressions as affecting our contact with other people, and the text explicitly refers to them as "tools" for influencing social interactions.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "However, she cautions that this effect only applies when an individual already has some background knowledge."
Why: The question asks about the limitations of using sleep to solve problems, which corresponds to the warning that this effect requires prior background knowledge.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "Dreams seem to be related to a reshuffling of memories, and indeed, it is often said that studying before sleep is a good way to retain information."
Why: The question mentions an activity before sleep (studying) helping with information recall (retaining information), matching this statement.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "Before falling asleep, the brain aims to acknowledge a thought and then move on to the next one. In reality, however, people tend to latch onto a single thought and ruminate on it, which can trigger feelings of regret and an adrenaline response, according to Stickgold."
Why: The question contrasts what the brain intends to do ("acknowledge a thought and then move on") with what people actually do ("latch onto a single thought and ruminate on it").

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "According to Barrett, all functions of the brain must have some practical purpose rooted in evolution and natural selection, which may explain why the brain uses dreams to break down, analyse, and solve problems."
Why: The question asks for an explanation of why we have dreams, which is answered by their evolutionary purpose rooted in problem-solving.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "To test whether or not sleep really does play a role in solving difficult problems, researchers at Northwestern University conducted a study in which they presented participants with a series of tricky, carefully designed puzzles, each of which participants had two minutes to figure out."
Why: The summary states that participants had to solve certain puzzles with a sound, and the text describes these as "tricky" puzzles presented during the experiment.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Their success rate improved across the board, but the most marked improvement was in puzzles that were associated with sound clips they had heard while sleeping, solving 32% of the sleep-cued puzzles, compared to only 21% of the uncued puzzles."
Why: The summary asks what improved the following morning, and the text directly states that the participants' "success rate" improved after sleeping and hearing the sound cues.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "A study on the benefits of napping, headed by Sara Mednick, assistant professor of psychiatry at the University of California, San Diego, and Denise Cai, a graduate student, revealed that rapid eye movement (REM) sleep enhances creative problem solving."
Why: The summary refers to Sara Mednick's study showing the benefits of REM sleep for creative outcomes, which the text identifies as "creative problem solving".

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "She believes that REM sleep does this because it stimulates associative networks, which allow the brain to make connections between unrelated concepts or ideas."
Why: The summary mentions associations between previously unlinked ideas, and the text uses the word "unrelated" to describe the concepts or ideas connected by the brain.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "The brain picks out emotions that occurred during or shortly after something happened and uses these memory cues to indicate that the event was important and needs to be analysed further."
Why: The summary states that the brain selects items connected to an event to determine importance, and the text specifies that these are "emotions".

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "While we sleep, the brain sorts, consolidates, and stores new information, and “walks through” memories of recent events."
Why: "walks through" memories means going over them, and distinguishing meaningful patterns from unhelpful background noise means differentiating between useful and trivial information.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "Getting up in the middle of the night to work on a problem is not particularly helpful, as it usually results in exhaustion without bringing one closer to a solution."
Why: Getting up in the middle of the night to work means staying up late or interrupting sleep, which Stickgold states is ineffective for solving problems.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "This research adds to a growing body of literature suggesting that sleep can reorganise information to facilitate problem-solving,” says Kristin Sanders, first author of the study and a doctoral student at Northwestern University."
Why: Sanders states that sleep reorganises information, which directly restates the idea that information related to a problem can be restructured during sleep.

title: Reading Passage 2 - The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:

title: Reading Passage 3 - A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages

title: Reading Passage 3 - A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:

Why: The writer argues that using a neutral word caused subjects to find little meaning and made the methodology lack validity, contradicting the idea that the choice was helpful.

title: Reading Passage 3 - A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages

title: Reading Passage 3 - A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages

title: Reading Passage 3 - Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
