title: Reading Passage 3 - Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The husband-and-wife team Frank and Lillian Gilbreth, and Henry Gantt (who advocated bonus pay, rather than threats, as a motivational tool), either tried to soften Taylor’s tactics or disdained them altogether, while trying to combine efficient processes with consideration for the workers."
Why: Option B restates this by noting they had a more sympathetic approach to the workers, contrasting with Taylor's bullying boss style by combining efficiency with consideration for employees.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Perhaps more than any other business management guru, she added new, substantive theories, which are still reflected in management practice today."
Why: Option A restates this as making a significant contribution to the development of management theory, corresponding to adding new, substantive theories that remain reflected in practice today.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Bottom-up management, he argues, is even worse than top-down; rather than limiting the potential abuses of managerial power, it cloaks such abuses in a false morality."
Why: The passage states that bottom-up management "cloaks such abuses in a false morality," meaning it is just as "abusive" as top-down management.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:

title: Reading Passage 3 - New Zealand Short Stories

title: Reading Passage 3 - The ability to communicate using language

title: Reading Passage 3 - The ability to communicate using language

title: Reading Passage 3 - The ability to communicate using language

title: Reading Passage 3 - The Pirah people of Brazil

title: Reading Passage 3 - The Pirah people of Brazil

title: Reading Passage 3 - The Pirah people of Brazil

title: Reading Passage 3 - The tuatara – past and future

title: Reading Passage 3 - The tuatara – past and future

title: Reading Passage 3 - The tuatara – past and future
explanation:

title: Reading Passage 3 - The tuatara – past and future

title: Reading Passage 3 - The tuatara – past and future

title: Reading Passage 3 - The tuatara – past and future

title: Reading Passage 3 - The tuatara – past and future

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams
explanation:

Why: Mammals and birds are specified as the types of living creatures that experience REM sleep.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "“Dreaming is a mental-health activity,” she says."
Why: Rosalind Cartwright's statement that dreaming is a "mental-health activity" links dreaming directly to psychological well-being.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "Since then, Solms has argued that medical diagnostic equipment like functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and positron emission tomography (PET), which helps researchers watch dreaming brains, might actually lend new support to Freud’s ideas because the parts of the brain that are most active during dreaming control emotion."
Why: This sentence explains how modern medical diagnostic tools (fMRI and PET) have provided new support (strengthened) Freud's theories about the brain.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams
explanation:

Quote: "Thousands of years ago, dreams were seen as messages from the gods, and in many cultures they are still considered prophetic, foretelling things to come."
Why: Option B restates the text's mention that dreams were considered "prophetic, foretelling things to come" in ancient times.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams
explanation:

Quote: "REM sleep heats up the brain and non-REM cools it off, Siegel says, and that could mean that the changing sleep cycles allow the brain to repair itself."
Why: Option D restates the scientist's finding that "REM sleep heats up the brain", meaning the temperature of the brain increases.

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Much less active during REM sleep is the prefrontal cortex, which is associated with logical thinking. That could explain why dreams in REM sleep often lack a coherent storyline."
Why: Option C restates that dreams lack a clear narrative because the "prefrontal cortex, which is associated with logical thinking" (reasoning) is "much less active" (less involved).

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Another active part of the brain in REM sleep is the anterior cingulate cortex, which detects differences or inconsistencies."
Why: Option A names the "anterior cingulate cortex", which the text identifies as active during REM sleep and which Eric Nofzinger believes is the reason people can "solve tricky problems in their dreams."

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams
explanation:

title: Reading Passage 3 - Unlocking the Mystery of Dreams
